## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Virocanajātaka* (Ja 143), translated as *The Shining*, is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection. According to the narrative framework preserved in its commentary, the Buddha delivered the tale while residing at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) in response to Devadatta's attempt to pose as a Buddha at Gayāsīsa [Fausböll 1877]. The *Dhammapada* commentary similarly notes that the Buddha related the *Vīraka*, *Kandagalaka*, and *Virocana* Jātakas on successive days in reference to Devadatta's career [Burlingame 1921].

In the tale of the past, a jackal meets a violent death when foolishly attempting to imitate the hunting prowess of a lion, embodying a classical pair of symbolic opposites found across ancient Indian literature [Bodhi 2003]. The canonical verse of the Jātaka (verse 139) mocks the ruined pretender whose skull is shattered and whose ribs are broken: *Lasī ca te nipphalitā... sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, ajja kho tvaṁ virocasīti* ("Your brains have oozed out... all your ribs are broken; today indeed you shine!") [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1877]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha explains that the doomed jackal was Devadatta, while the lion was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1877].
